speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not going to delay the house long. I rise to say that the C.C.F. party in the house welcomes the presentation of the international wheat agreement. We have long urged that our country should endeavour in every way possible to co-operate with other producing nations in bringing about an agreement that would give some stability to the production of this important cereal.
In connection with the agreement the hon. member for Neepawa (Mr. Bracken), who has just taken his seat, has said many of the things that I had thought of saying. Therefore I am not going to repeat anything he has said. I am going to point out however that when the British wheat agreement was made on Thursday, August 15, 1946, in giving support to that agreement on behalf of this party I made the statement that in the event of the cost of production rising for the next few years, as it might do, largely because of the government's failure to maintain ceilings on other goods, any difference there might be between what the farmer received for his wheat and the increased cost of production should be made up out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada. On that occasion I added that if this occurred, and prices rose, a compensatory adjustment should be made.

At that time the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in reply made the statement that just as we had arranged to set aside some $200 million for the support of other agricultural products, so a similar provision might be made. He drew to the attention of the house the fact that owing to the change in the tariff of the United States he anticipated that the cost of farm machinery, and so on, would come down. We all know that that did not happen, and that the costs of production rose.
Western farmers, bound to this agreement, an agreement freely entered into with the support of all parties in this house, had to accept a price which was much lower than they could have obtained in some other way -although I do not agree that the price that was obtained on the Chicago market was what could be called a world price. However I do think that the price might have been considerably higher than the price which he actually obtained for the wheat which he sold under the British agreement.
And, Mr. Speaker, I want to draw this once again to the attention of the house, that from 1943 to 1947 the wheat growers of Canada subsidized flour and bread that was used in the homes of Canadian people from one end of the country to the other. No matter what the price of wheat was, it will be recalled that wheat was sold to the millers for domestic consumption at a price of approximately 78 cents a bushel when farmers received a price lower than the average wheat price.
Consequently I suggest to the house tonight that, in spite of the fact that there is a sliding scale downward for the wheat during the four years of the life of this world wheat agreement, namely from $1.95 a bushel down to $1.20 a bushel, we should guarantee to the producer, regardless of what the price of wheat may be, under this agreement, an average price over the four years of this agreement of $1.85 a bushel for the wheat he produces throughout the four years of the agreement. Some may ask, will that not involve a levy on the people of Canada? It depends of course on the price that we get for our wheat, but it is conceivable that it may involve such a levy. The point I am making is that during the five years 1943 to 1947 inclusive, the wheat growers of Canada -and of course they are for the most part the prairie farmers-assumed a major responsibility of providing cheap flour and cheap bread for the people of Canada. I contend that, having done that for those five seasons, they are now entitled to a compensatory adjustment, if you like to call it that, during the four years of the life of this agreement. I make that suggestion in all seriousness because I think it is one that is worthy of consideration by the government at this
International Wheat Agreement time in justice to the men who accepted the responsibility of providing that cheaper wheat and flour, apart altogether from any so-called loss that may have occurred through shipping wheat to the United Kingdom at a price lower than they might otherwise have obtained.
Having said that, I want to say that we welcome this agreement because the outlook is none too good for many of our agricultural products, including this great cereal grain. Last year the United States produced a great crop, and it is now estimated that the United States, with modern methods and machinery, with the land now under cultivation, and with a disinclination to grow certain crops that have been grown in the past, is geared to produce something like 1,300 million bushels of wheat of all kinds in an average good year. If we remember that the consumption of wheat domestically in the United States is usually something slightly over 700 million bushels, that means that between 500 million and 600 million bushels of wheat will be available for export to the markets of the world.
Consequently an agreement of this description, which guarantees to Canada at least an assured export market of approximately 200 million bushels of wheat, is worth while. Even if the adjustment referred to by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has to be made, and we have to take a portion of that adjustment, the amount that Canada will export will still be in the neighbourhood of 200 million bushels. That will give some stability to our western agriculture although I realize, of course, that in a normal year we produce and export more than the amount that is allotted to us under this international agreement. None the less, in the uncertain world in which we live, and as the hon. member for Neepawa (Mr. Bracken) has said, with two great potential wheat-producing countries outside this agreement, the U.S.S.R. and the Argentine republic, with countries that up to now were importing, such as France, entering into the export field, and with the opening up of vast areas of semi-arid land in North Africa for the growing of wheat, I think we are wise as a country to participate in an agreement of this description.
Our western farmers have hoped for years for stability. They accepted the British wheat agreement because they preferred stability to speculation. This agreement is going to give them stability at least to a degree which they have lacked in the past. To my mind such an agreement must end the speculation in this great cereal grain, and it is another reason why this party has been
2786	HOUSE OF
International Wheat Agreement justified throughout the years in asking for the elimination of speculation in all the people's foodstuffs, and particularly for the closing of the Winnipeg grain exchange.
I do not propose to prolong the discussion.
I merely rose to make the suggestion that our western farmers having contributed to the food supply of our country and of the world both directly and indirectly, having accepted the responsibility during the years 1943 to 1947 of bearing a substantial part of the cost of subsidizing bread and flour for the people of this country-and they still do to some extent-and of supplying our great sister nation of the British commonwealth with food on a basis that we agreed upon in 1946, the government should now not only consider making, but actually proceed to make, what is in effect a compensatory adjustment, which was not given to our farmers during the war, and which we asked for when the British wheat agreement was under discussion. With this request we support the agreement, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I had intended to speak on this motion at some length, but the situation being what it is I shall make my remarks quite brief. At the outset let me say that we in this group believe in the principle of long-term international food agreements. As we stated last year, we believe in them because we believe they are in the interests of both the producer and the consumer in that they help to guarantee to the consumer adequate supplies of food at a fair price, and they are in the interests of the producer in that they help to guarantee adequate markets at a fair price.
I think one of the most important points is that it makes it possible in good years to build up a reserve of food to take care of poor crop years without those reserves being used as an excuse to force prices down, as has invariably been the case under the so-called open market system. Of course we logically believe that the right way to handle wheat to meet our commitments would be under the 100 per cent wheat board. On the other hand, we regret that this measure contains some of the same weaknesses that were contained in its predecessor brought down in the house last year, weaknesses that may very well undermine the agreement and force certain nations to cancel their purchases under it, not because they want to, but because they may well be compelled to do so.
I think the main general criticism of longterm international agreements is that, in trying to set a price for the future, you are merely guessing what that price should be. True, we do not set a definite price for any one year, but we do set a ceiling and a floor, and it is just a question whether or not the 

level of the ceiling and the floor that we set is the correct one. For instance, as an argument against the international wheat agreement many people will refer us to the British wheat agreement under which farmers have to date suffered quite severe losses. I want to point out one big difference between the international wheat agreement and the British wheat agreement. The British wheat agreement was not a straight business deal. When that agreement was brought before the house the government asked support for it on the ground that it was a moral obligation to help Great Britain get wheat at a reasonable price. Hon. members of this group supported it on that basis, but when we supported it we pointed out time and again that the responsibility was not that of the Canadian farmer but of the Canadian people and that any losses that might be sustained as a result of that agreement should be borne by the Canadian people as a whole and not passed on to the Canadian farmers. Up to date the full cost of that agreement has been borne by the Canadian farmers.
According to a return tabled in the house, in the first two years of the agreement the farmers lost over $353 million. At the same time the cost of subsidizing the Canadian consumer up to December last amounted to over $190 million, making a total loss of over $543 million which has been borne entirely by the Canadian farmer. There will be more losses in the third year. It may be argued that in the fourth year there may be some gains, but in view of the fact that under the international wheat agreement there is a floor of $1.50, the gain cannot be very great. There are 140 million bushels being sold to Great Britain at $2 and with a floor of $1.50 there can be a gain of only 50 cents per bushel, which would amount to $70 million. That would not be very much to offset a loss of some $550 million.
I think the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) should make a statement to the house of the policy of the government with regard to these losses. Is the government going to pay the farmers for these losses after July 31, 1950, the end of the agreement? Or will an equivalent amount be placed in a reserve to help stabilize prices in the future? The government might adopt the suggestion of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) and place a floor under wheat prices during the life of the international wheat agreement of $1.75. The farmers are entitled to hear from the government what their policy is going to be in regard to the heavy losses they have sustained on behalf of the people of Canada as a whole.
It is well to remember that the international wheat agreement is not being

brought in as a moral obligation; it is being brought down as a straight business agreement. Under this agreement we are trying to estimate what the price should be in the future. In setting the ceilings and floors that we have, we may be right. On the other hand, we may be wrong. I do not doubt for one minute that when the government agreed to the British wheat agreement they thought that the price of wheat was going to go down; they never thought that the price was going to go up in the way it did. But they guessed wrongly. How do we know that a similar mistake is not being made today?
We feel that in trying to set a price for the future some consideration should be given to the price level of other commodities. In other words, we feel that we should set a price for the first year in relation to the price level of other commodities and then tie that price to the general price level of the importing countries so that, if that general price level goes down, the price of wheat goes down. If on the other hand the general price level goes up, the price of wheat will also go up. In that way you would be balancing your exports against imports and you would be getting an international parity price for your wheat which would make it a comparatively easy thing for a government to maintain a national parity price.
The second thing I want to refer to is the method of payment under the agreement. We are to be paid by the European nations in Canadian dollars. If any European nation suffers an unbalance of trade and is unable to meet its commitments in Canadian dollars it will have the right to be released from the obligation to buy its quota of wheat. That is the situation in existence today and that is the situation that is likely to continue for a few years. There is every likelihood that some of the European nations will not be able to meet their commitments and will have to seek permission to be released from their obligation to buy wheat under the agreement.
We feel that it would be a far safer procedure for Canada to agree to accept payment in sterling and then we could use our surplus sterling balances to trade with European nations on a multilateral basis. In that way we would be making it much easier for the European nations to buy our wheat and at the same time we would have currency with which to buy European products.
I regret that to date no legislation has been placed on the statute books of Canada to guarantee the stabilization of farm products on a permanent basis. We have the international wheat agreement for four years with prices at quite a low level. We have no guarantee that losses under the British wheat agreement will be made up and there 29087-176

International Wheat Agreement is absolutely no guarantee regarding the prices of other commodities. Since 1942 the farmers have been accepting a loss on the sale of their products and they have been told that that is necessary in the name of stabilization. Up to the present time the government's program of stabilization has been to reduce the prices of farm commodities. As I say, there is on the statute books no legislation of a permanent nature to guarantee that. The Agricultural Prices Support Act is the only act that deals with that question and it expires on March 31, 1950.
So I hope the Prime Minister will see fit before parliament is dissolved to make some declaration regarding the government's policy on this matter.

speechtext:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve the North Atlantic treaty signed at Washington on April 4, 1949, and that this house do approve the same.
He said: I deem it a great privilege to submit to this house a resolution to approve the North Atlantic treaty. I shall not take very many minutes in doing so because it was my privilege to recommend to the house on March 28 a resolution approving the attendance of a Canadian delegation at Washington to sign a North Atlantic treaty along the lines of a draft which was in the hands of the members at the time the resolution was adopted.
The treaty was signed in Washington on April 4 and photostatic copies of the treaty with the signatures were tabled in this house some days ago. The treaty is in exactly the same form as the draft which was before the members of this house when they approved the attendance of a Canadian delegation at Washington for the purpose of signing such a treaty. It was signed in that form by the twelve countries whose adherence was looked upon as essential to the constitution of a group of democratic nations that could, by their co-operation, favour the economic, social, political and military security of each other.
Since it was signed I have had the opportunity of discussing it with many Canadians in different parts of the country. Among all those with whom I discussed it I have found the same unanimity that was manifested in this house on March 28, 1949. I think it will be the feeling of a great many of us that the signing of it has already produced some easing of the tension in this cold war from which we have been suffering over the last four years. I was quite encouraged to find that practically everyone in Canada recognized that if we really wish to have peace we have to be prepared to do our part to see that peace is maintained in the world. If peace were not maintained in the world there would seem to be little prospect of our own people avoiding the repercussions of war. I hope that will prove to be the experience of this country and of the nations represented by the signatories to the treaty over the whole period for which the treaty is made.
I merely want to add that we still hope that the effect of this arrangement between the twelve democratic nations that have signed the North Atlantic treaty will show the rest of the world that it is possible for human beings to make an arrangement that

will secure to themselves, and to their fellows, the advantages that were promised to men of good will in this world. In time it will perhaps give place to that which we would all, I am sure, unanimously welcome, that is to say a similar satisfactory arrangement embracing all the nations who were parties to the San Francisco pact, and make that instrument the effective organ for world peace that it was intended to be when it was signed in San Francisco four years ago.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is very little to add to what has already been said here in support of the pact. At the time the draft pact was before this house there was practically unanimity here in support of that draft. As the Prime Minister has pointed out, the pact signed in Washington is in the exact terms of the draft we have already approved. The signing of the pact carries certain obligations which must be recognized and fulfilled by every one of the signatory nations if the pact is to achieve the high purpose for which it has been signed. It not only embraces the expression of joint action to preserve peace, but it involves also the joint action of those nations in the economic field which is of very great importance and which will require positive action on the part of the signatory nations.
So far as Canada is concerned, along with each of the other nations which have signed that pact, there is the obligation to join with the military strength of the countries for the preservation of peace as a great partnership dedicated to that purpose. There is also the obligation to follow a course in the economic field which has its place in strengthening this association. I trust that Canada, as one of the signatory nations, will at all times bear in mind that, while our ultimate hope undoubtedly is that, from the sound basis of this pact, a new attitude may develop which ultimately will lead to friendship even with Russia itself, in the meantime there is no illusion about the fact that the joint strength of these nations is being placed before the world as a challenge to further encroachment of the soviet empire. When we recognize that fact I believe it is essential that we be prepared to put forward our position and to express the hope that others will share the same point of view, and that, with regard to trading with Russia, there will be taken a position which will make it perfectly certain that through trading with Russia we will not at any time increase their war potential or their ability to strengthen their own position in confronting the free nations of the world.
I think we should also remember that Russia has followed a course of infiltration, and has achieved as much by that method of
North Atlantic Treaty
infiltration as by actual military power. I believe that we should recognize the fact that it would be to their advantage to undermine the economic strength of the free nations of the west, and that we should not enter into any trading arrangements with them which will have the effect of undermining the economic structure of the free nations which are joined in the defence of their own freedom.
I do not think I need to enlarge upon that matter, because this would include a definite understanding that there will not be supplied to Russia any aircraft, any war equipment, machine tools which could be used for war potential, the great electric generators and dynamos that can supply the war potential of the factories which would be dependent upon them, or in fact to supply them with any of those things which can directly or indirectly increase their military strength, until they have offered us some gesture of good faith which would justify us in extending the hand of friendship to them.
I think we should also bear in mind that since this pact was signed in Washington an event has taken place which has importance to those of us who live in the British commonwealth and also immense importance to those nations which signed that pact; because it needs to be emphasized not only within our country but to the whole world that, in that document which was signed a few days ago in London, an unprecedented relationship between the east and the west was established where, for the first time in the long history of mankind, three great Asiatic nations have freely associated themselves as free nations with the other nations of the commonwealth in the joint responsibility of preserving the principles of freedom to which we are all committed.
By this new expression of the fellowship of those who believe in the common principles of freedom upon which the British commonwealth has been established, they have said that all of them recognize their obligation to preserve those principles; and that includes not only Britain, Canada, Australia, South Africa and New Zealand, but India with its 400 million people, Pakistan with nearly 100 million more, and Ceylon with its millions. Those nations now stand side by side with us in supporting the principles of freedom which we assert as the basis of our signing the Atlantic pact. So through this very document which was signed in London, the implications of the Atlantic pact have been carried to Asia where, confronting Russia itself, are five hundred million people who, through their association in earlier years, have learned the idea of the British common law and of that concept of freedom which we all share.

North Atlantic Treaty
Out of these two documents, as long as the nations carry into full effect the undertaking they have given, we may well see the beginning of one of the most solid and most hopeful periods of peace that the world has known.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say in all sincerity that the members of my party-and we feel also the people of Canada-look upon this pact from the point of view of the possibilities of the preservation of peace. In

supporting this pact it is our sincere belief that it may be a step toward peace, and not a step toward war.
We believe that a third world war would be so catastrophic as to dissolve our very civilization, and to render null and void all that has been accomplished by our race over the centuries. This is an age which has within it methods of destruction at its disposal, such as the use of atomic materials capable of bringing about the tremendous results of which we saw evidence in the closing months of the last war. We saw that whole cities could be wiped out, large numbers of people destroyed, along with their means of living. We trust that such calamities will not occur again.
It is on these grounds that we support the pact, believing that the nations who are signatory to it will not attempt to abandon the hope and the promise that lies within the United Nations as a centre where we may discuss our problems and reach agreements. This is important to our people, and we hope that that will be the result of the pact when we support it. In this pact the signatories are committed to preserving the democratic way of life and to enlarging the principles of democracy, the principles of humanity, within the states that are now agreed as to the pact.
It is necessary at this time to direct the attention of the Canadian people, and of the Canadian government, to one of the signatories of the pact. I speak of Portugal. In Portugal for more than thirty years there have been no free trade unions. speechtext: I am quite prepared to give the Minister of Labour a talk on Russia. He has asked for it, so here goes. I say that the unfortunate people of Russia did not have the good fortune to pass through the stages of civilization which we in the western nations have. I point out to my hon. friend that the iron curtain is not a new thing, that it existed during the middle ages. A study of history will show that the maritime nations of Europe, even before machines were invented and power machinery went into operation, through trade by sea were enabled to enjoy a much easier life than those nations which are cut off from the sea, and which lie between Asia and the west coast.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF TREATY SIGNED AT WASHINGTON ON APRIL 4, 1949
speechtext: Is the hon. member apologizing for Russia?

The eastern nations of Europe have had difficulties which we have never had to undergo. Right up to the year of the opening of the first world war, 1914, they were still living under a feudal system while

North Atlantic Treaty
we were living under an advanced and modern capitalist system. I should like to point out to my hon. friend that the results of that were that when the transition had to be made from feudal to capitalist methods of production, instead of having the good fortune of that gradual evolution and development of public institutions that we have had, they had to make their change by violence, and they have reached not the promised land of democracy but the horrors of a national dictatorship. I suggest to my hon. friend that he try to think of the people of Russia not with hatred, not with contempt, and I suggest that international peace will be much better served if my hon. friend is inspired by the sentiments I am trying to voice than by the deliberate desire to hold in contempt the unfortunate people of eastern Europe.

May I remind hon. members that our point of view on the North Atlantic pact is much more likely than their own to be in line with the thoughts of modern people.

If it pleases hon. members to interrupt, it also pleases me to continue speaking. I was at the point where I was trying to point out to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) why he should regard the people of eastern Europe with sympathy instead of contempt. I will proceed along those lines. The situation which occurred in 1917 was that these people, 82 per cent illiterate, unable to read or write, and many of them unable to absorb more than a few simple ideas displayed to them through slogans by the Bolshevist party which assumed power, overthrowing as they did the monstrous fascist and czarist regime, instead of receiving co-operation, the humanitarian and brotherly treatment to which they were entitled in their hour of need, were surrounded by a cordon sanitaire with the net result that there was sown in them that distrust which we are reaping today when we meet with their representatives in the United Nations. Instead of being able to co-operate we are constantly being faced with the utmost hostility. The road to international peace lies not only in a change of heart on the part of the Russians but in a change of heart on the part of our representatives.
Our attitude towards these people, who we are being persuaded are our enemies, must be changed to one of peaceful approach to world problems. We must never give up the effort to co-operate. The signing of pacts cannot in itself prevent war and it is necessary for us to stress the peaceful attributes of this North Atlantic pact, to stress the desire on the part of the nations with which we are affiliated in this pact, on the part of our own government and our own people, to do what we can to reconcile the differences, great as they may be, between the unfortunate dictatorships of eastern Europe and the progressive democracies of the western world.
I suggest to members of the government that if we were able through negotiation with this great power, which covers one-sixth of

the earth's surface, to impress upon them the desire we have to help them to raise their standard of living to the high peaks on which the North American standard of living now rests, we might then be able to have peaceful relations with them. I would say that a million refrigerators, radios and Ford cars would do more good in eastern Europe than a million bayonets. Upon this government rests the responsibility of saving millions of our lives as well as millions of Russian lives through their attitude toward the eastern world.
I did not rise in order to lecture my friends across the way, because there is no great difference between us in our admiration for democratic principles. However, I earnestly ask them to take the stand that this pact must be enlarged to include more nations than are now signatories to it. We in this group would like to see every democratic nation on the globe become a signatory to this pact. If it is possible to stretch the Atlantic community to include Italy, which is in the centre of the Mediterranean, perhaps it will be possible to extend it to include India, Australia, New Zealand and many of the social democratic countries outside the North Atlantic area.
Perhaps it will be possible for us to negotiate to the extent where we can get some of these countries which today are considered to be under the influence of Russia to join with us in this North Atlantic pact. It might be possible for us to include Yugoslavia, which has shown recently that it is not prepared to submit to the economic dictatorship of Russia.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF TREATY SIGNED AT WASHINGTON ON APRIL 4, 1949
speechtext: Why not Russia?

subtopic: APPROVAL OF TREATY SIGNED AT WASHINGTON ON APRIL 4, 1949
speechtext:
Somebody says, "Why not Russia?" If this is a pact for peace, then why not Russia? If it is a pact for war, let us say so. I do not believe that it is a pact for war; I believe it is a pact for peace. That is why I want to extend it, for the forces of peace can never be too large.
I have only one more remark to make. As did many hon. gentlemen here, I served in the last war. For a time I served in Italy and I had the opportunity to visit the ruins of Pompeii. I saw there many marvellous things that I never believed had existed in a civilization so far removed in time from our own. I saw copper pipes, heating systems, baths, public clubs and evidence of a high standard of living. I saw many mechanical devices which have long since passed away.
I went from the old city of Pompeii to the modern city and I saw their hovels in which people were living in one room with narrow windows, without either hot or cold water and with absolutely no sanitary facilities. Many
North Atlantic Treaty
of them had very little to eat. In that picture lies a lesson. If we can devise ways to prevent another world war we may continue as a civilization. If we cannot prevent a third world war, then a state of affairs demonstrated by a comparison of modern Pompeii with the Pompeii of a former civilization may well be upon us.
I ask my hon. friends to learn the lessons of history, for they are well worth learning. They may represent the difference between survival and oblivion for the civilization in which we live.

Mr. Speaker, the other day I read a brief communique of the C.C.F. party to the effect that some of their members were not present to vote on the Atlantic pact because they had left after I had started to speak. I am wondering if the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Probe) was one of them. There was that communique, whether it was official or informal I do not know.
I am speaking at the invitation of the leader of that group for whom I have great respect and admiration as a debater. He wanted to know if I had some reason for expressing an opinion on the pact. I have one reason which I think will surprise him greatly. I want to know what members of his party went out when I started to speak and I want to know their reasons for opposing the pact.
Having listened to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Young), I find that I know no more now that he has finished than I did before he rose. I would like to see him fitted with a glass skull so that I could see how his brain was working. I cannot understand the manner in which he considers a matter of such importance as the Atlantic pact. He spoke about Portugal and about Yugoslavia. We are not in Portugal and we are not in Yugoslavia. What we know of those countries we learn from the press. I have no particular friends in Portugal and I have no private source of information in Yugoslavia.

We are under the roof of a house because we do not want the rain to fall upon us when we are sleeping, and so on. It is the same instinct of self-preservation.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF TREATY SIGNED AT WASHINGTON ON APRIL 4, 1949
speechtext:
I will not say anything about my own appreciation of what he said, sir. When we have listened to what has been said about this pact by the leaders of the various groups in the house, and then when we listen to a speech such as that delivered by the member on a matter of such importance, which concerns the life of all Canadians, may I say, speaking as a member of parliament, that I am deeply offended. It is a matter that must be considered seriously and I am sure that if the hon. gentleman does not mend his ways, if he continues speaking in that manner, he will do considerable harm to his party in spite of the very fine speeches that are made by the leader of the group and by so many able members who belong to it. I do not say that as a matter of censorship, but as a member of parliament who wants to do his duty-a duty he has to perform as a matter of trust.
Just one more word, Mr. Speaker. The matter is serious. The other day I said that international sovereignty was nonsense and it has been reported wrongly in Hansard. I said what I believed. I do not believe in international sovereignty. I believe also that instead of having pacts made in other countries by the former major powers, we should have our own pact with all other nations of the world.
But, Mr. Speaker, there is something else that I want to stress before you. It is that for a long time I have complained of the fact of the distinction between major powers and little countries. In the security council of the United Nations, Canada was there in turn. But in the United Nations organization everything was decided by the major powers. Countries like Canada, Australia and others had their say only at times, we had no status of equality, whilst in the Atlantic pact all are equal. For me the Atlantic pact is much superior to the United Nations organization. That is one point.
There is another point. I remember that my friend the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), the leader of the Social Credit group, my good friend Tommy Church from Toronto, who is probably being nominated tonight as candidate in this coming election, and myself were called irresponsible by a dirty paper of Montreal because we were telling the truth. We were saying that the United Nations organization was going on the rocks. I compliment my friend the leader of the Social Credit group and my good friend

the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) for having joined me in protesting on that occasion. Were we right or were we not? Who was irresponsible? Was it the members of parliament who foresaw what was going to happen?-namely the downfall of the United Nations, to be replaced by a new organization, the Atlantic pact, which I hope will work well.
I have been invited to speak, Mr. Speaker, and I do so, although I do not intend to speak for any great length of time. The time of reckoning has come. We were good Canadian citizens and we were patriots in saying then what has happened since.
I want to be protected. As the United Nations organization has proved to be a failure and as some great nations of the world, especially our powerful neighbour, the United States of America, the countries of the British commonwealth, France, Benelux, some Scandinavian countries, Portugal and others are joining together for defence and protection, I will be for it. I want to give the Atlantic pact a chance. I do not want to stay behind. In these troubled times we need some protection against nations that may invade our country at any time. But I do not want the rule of brass hats; and I hope that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) will tell the generals, who have been touring the country exciting the people and speaking as warmongers, to stop doing so. I hope that the work of the united nations who have signed the Atlantic pact will be effective, that in the near future the atmosphere will be cleared, and that we shall have peace throughout the world.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before any motion is put I should like to make a suggestion which I think may facilitate proceedings. Before the dinner hour the house was in committee, and supply was being discussed. Quite contrary to the statement made by someone who spoke just before dinner, and who assumed responsibility for indicating what our decision had been, it is not our intention to prevent supply.	*
We have presented our objections. We have, I believe, covered them fully. We have stated what our case is, and we have called for a vote, which was in the nature of a want of confidence vote, and one which expresses our position. I believe that if we now went back into the committee stage we might advance with supply and then be that much closer to the proceedings of tomorrow.
In saying this I should like to explain why I regard this as the desirable course. The government has assumed the responsibility of announcing dissolution; and that course, it is recognized, has to be followed. I need not add to the opinion I have already expressed as to the procedure which has been followed -to do so would be only to repeat what is already on the record.
The business of the people must go on in any event during the course of the election campaign, and for a sufficient time beyond that to make it possible to carry on the business before parliament can reassemble. Therefore the only alternative with which the house is confronted is the alternative of supply or of proceeding with governor general's warrants. I am convinced, myself, that there are certain limitations upon the use of governor general's warrants, which may not have been fully recognized, and I feel there is no occasion for us to create any uncertainty as to the fulfilment of public
business while this election campaign is under way, and for sufficient time thereafter to call together a new parliament.
Therefore, having stated our case, we will facilitate the proceedings which are before us.

Mr. Speaker, I was going to ask the Prime Minister if it was the intention to move that the house sit tomorrow. If it is the intention that we pass such a motion, then may I say that this has been a very long and very arduous day. These have been two days, indeed, in which we have had to listen to long speeches on occasion; and I wish to say, Mr. Speaker, that I think we would advance the business of the house more if we adjourned now and got a good night's rest.
I am not in favour of falling in with the suggestion made by some who have taken up a tremendous amount of time in this house during the past few days. I am going to object to the house sitting beyond this hour.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The hon. member said that if a motion was made to sit tomorrow he would feel that he would have to object to sitting further this evening. A motion was moved at 5.45 this afternoon providing that the house sit tomorrow at eleven o'clock, and that the intermissions and order of business be the same as today. That motion was agreed to. There remains the matter of supply and third reading of the bills that have been reported from the standing committee.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Also the committee stage on those bills.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The committee stage and third reading of the bills that have just been reported from the select standing committee. I would not imagine that would take very much time. It would not really relieve members of the necessity of coming back tomorrow because there has to be royal assent to these matters, and there will have to be consideration in another place of the bill based upon the resolution for interim supply, so that in any event we shall have to come back at eleven o'clock tomorrow. The suggestion made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) that his group would facilitate the voting of such supply as is required for the essential business of the country during the period necessary for an election, and to call parliament together, is welcomed by this side of the house, and I wish to extend to him a word of appreciation of that offer of co-operation. If there is objection to proceeding any longer tonight, perhaps the leader of the opposition will understand, and we can take up these mat-

ters when we meet at eleven o'clock. I would hope that the tentative arrangements that have been made to ask the deputy of His Excellency the Governor General to attend for royal assent at twelve o'clock noon can still be carried out.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to say more than that I think most of the members look reasonably fresh, and after all there will be certain advantages, I think, from the point of view of handling the business of the government itself if these bills are dealt with now. They can be disposed of very quickly and will then be ready for final disposition tomorrow. I suggest that we proceed in the committee stage.
I am a little bit tired of the attitude adopted by the leader of the opposition.
You are always tired of it.
You are not the only people who can talk here although you have been going about it quite aimlessly for the last three or four days.
You were tired before you came here.

I am not tired enough not to oppose the suggestion made now. I was the one who pointed out before the dinner recess that from the attitude of the official opposition it was quite apparent that they were going to oppose interim supply.
Wrong.

Of course I was wrong. I was wrong until it was pointed out to the official opposition-
Business of the House
You are always wrong.

I was wrong until I pointed out to the official opposition that if they persisted in refusing to vote interim supply they could not stop the government going to the country, that the government would have to carry on the affairs of the country by the use of governor general's warrants, and that it was much better that parliament should vote supply in an orderly way, and thus enable the government to carry on the business of the country in an orderly way. I am glad that my friends have seen the light. It is just about time. After carrying on for the last three days as if the debate was a debate on the budget or some other such general debate it is sheer impudence to ask the house to sit after this hour tonight.
I am not going to extend this debate except to dispose of the statement that it was sheer impudence. That, of course, is so ridiculous that it need not be discussed-
It is true.

-except to point out that this house went into supply only yesterday, not three days ago, and that we have been discussing a matter of $600 million for a little over twenty-four hours. We are prepared to facilitate the course of the proceedings.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think hon. members will agree that we can perhaps finish in less time tomorrow than if we try to do so tonight. I therefore move that the house adjourn, and that the business for tomorrow be, first of all, interim supply and then consideration of the bills reported by the standing committee.
